# Select

Run your company with AI agents that earn their autonomy.

Agents of any kind — developers, marketers, support, sales — work in an organization you design. Every result is checked by code against a delivery contract, and an agent stops needing your approval only once its verified record shows it can — per task type, revocable at any time.

> Status: 0.2. Accounts, guided setup, local IMAP/SMTP mail tests, routines and the verification loop are covered by end-to-end tests. Docker images build and the Compose stack starts successfully in Ubuntu GitHub Actions CI. Real model API calls have not been verified yet: see Limits .

## Why Select

Multi-agent orchestrators let you decide in advance what agents may do alone. Select replaces that guess with evidence:

- Delivery contracts. Each task type has a YAML contract. The system runs its checks itself and keeps a receipt — contract version and hash, every check, the evidence. A model never declares that a check passed.

- Autonomy earned per agent and task type. Supervised → sampled → autonomous after a streak of verified successes; back to supervised at the first blocking failure or human correction.

- Limits the score never overrides. Payments, contracts, taxes and hiring are always supervised, in code.

- An honest counter. The share of work finished without a person is always shown next to the rate of errors people found afterwards.

- No invented numbers. Every value carries its source; a quantity that is not in the customer's e-mail fails verification.

Both diagrams are SVG and can be reviewed or edited directly in the repository.

## What it does

These four come from the end-to-end test run against local IMAP and SMTP test servers ( E2E_SCREENSHOTS_DIR ); the others are the demo company. All are real captures.

These are real Playwright screenshots of Select running locally with fictional demo data . No external model provider or mailbox is connected in this capture session.

## Quickstart

Requirements: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) or Docker Engine with Compose (Linux).

git clone https://github.com/Kirby54/Select.git select cd select ./start.sh # Windows: .\start.ps1

The script writes .env with random secrets (keep a copy), starts the containers and opens http://localhost:3000 , where the first visit creates your account. Without the script: cp .env.example .env , set the secrets, docker compose up --build .

No API key yet? Open the demo company from the account menu and press Run demo week .

Five-minute guide: docs/getting-started.md . Development setup without Docker: docs/installation.md .

## How autonomy works

Default promotion thresholds are 20 and 50 verified successes in a row — starting hypotheses to calibrate, not proven values . An e-mail to an address that never wrote to you always goes to a person. Details: docs/autonomy.md .

## A contract

id : support_reply version : 1 title : Support reply risk : medium required : [to, subject, body] checks : - id : recipient_from_message rule : provenance # the address must be the one that wrote to us params : { fields: [to] } - id : no_unauthorised_promises rule : forbidden_phrases params : { field: body, phrases: ["refund", "discount", "guarantee"] } approval : mode : by_autonomy external_action : send_email

More in docs/verification.md .

## Architecture

Next.js 16 web app → FastAPI API → PostgreSQL 16, with a worker on a durable PostgreSQL job queue that runs agents, reads mailboxes, sends approved e-mail and fires routines. select-verify is a separate Python library with no database or network access. See docs/architecture.md and the interface's design system .

## Security

Agents never hold a permission to send, pay or sign; the server applies the approval rules and sends. External content is treated as data and checked against stored sources. Passwords use Argon2id; sessions live in an HttpOnly cookie with an anti-forgery header; provider keys and mailbox passwords are encrypted. Read docs/security.md and docs/deployment.md before opening Select to a network.

## Tests

make test # Python verifier/API tests on PostgreSQL plus frontend unit tests make e2e # Playwright UI scenarios against a running stack

e2e/complete.spec.ts (4 more scenarios) runs on a password-mode stack with the local mail servers of scripts/dev-mail.py : first owner, guided setup, a real IMAP mailbox, an e-mail triaged, routed, quoted, approved and sent once over SMTP (the .eml file is checked), a weekly routine seen from a New York browser on Paris time, and an invited colleague joining.

## Verify a real model (optional)

The CI tests use network doubles, not real provider keys. Before connecting production data, use the explicit live-provider probe with your own test credentials . It sends a harmless fixed JSON-generation prompt and reports whether the chosen model returns the expected result. It never stores the key or accesses company data. Real-provider compatibility is not yet certified by the maintainers.

## Benchmarks

None published yet. The protocol ( autonomy-bench : same tasks and models, autonomy rate and undetected-error rate side by side, compared with a single agent and with Paperclip) is in bench/README.md . Until it runs, Select makes no comparative claim. Feature parity is tracked honestly in docs/parity.md .

## Limits

- Provider calls have not been exercised against real paid-model APIs (no keys in CI). An Ollama-compatible localhost HTTP stub is used to test the full worker, deterministic verification and approval pipeline; it does not execute a real model.

- Docker : GitHub Actions builds both images, starts PostgreSQL, API, worker and web with Compose, and reaches the API health endpoint through the web proxy on Ubuntu. The start.sh script itself was tested with a stand-in Docker CLI; real macOS/Windows installations and start.ps1 have not been exercised in CI.

- Mailboxes were tested against local IMAP and SMTP servers, not yet at a real provider. No OAuth: Microsoft 365 and Outlook.com cannot connect yet; Gmail needs an app password.

- Agents write text and structured results through model APIs. Code-change proposals can be checked for basic diff structure and sent to mandatory human review, but no repository code is edited, executed or pushed by Select. There is no isolated Claude Code or Codex runtime yet. See review-only code proposals .

- Attachments are not read; quotes are sent as e-mail text, without a PDF.

- No e-invoice : the invoice draft is not an XRechnung or ZUGFeRD file and is never presented as compliant. Businesses exempt from VAT ( franchise en base ) are not handled properly yet.

- No single sign-on, two-factor authentication, plugins or sandboxed code execution.

## Contributing

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md . Good first contributions: a new contract for a task type you know, or a new deterministic rule — each with one accepted and one rejected example.

## Roadmap

- Verify with real model keys and real mailboxes; keep Docker startup, recovery and tests green across supported environments.

- Coding-agent runtimes: run Claude Code or Codex in a code workspace, verify with the project's tests, approve the exact diff.

- Run without Docker (embedded database), like a one-command install.

- Quote PDFs, attachments, OAuth mailboxes, VAT-exempt businesses.

- Run autonomy-bench and publish the raw results.

The application ( apps/ ) is licensed under AGPL-3.0-only ( LICENSE ). The select-verify library is licensed under Apache-2.0 ( packages/select-verify/LICENSE ) so that other tools can adopt delivery contracts freely.

Questions and ideas: GitHub Discussions. Bugs: GitHub Issues. Vulnerabilities: privately, see SECURITY.md .

# Infinix — Local Autonomous Agent for Windows and Linux

> ⚠️ Project Status: ABANDONED / BASE FOR COMMUNITY. This project is no longer actively maintained by the original creator. The codebase is released as an open-source foundation for anyone to fork, improve, modify, or build upon. The only requirement: your derivative work must also remain free and open-source (GPL-3.0).

> Original Creator: Moonyeep - Built with Manus AI, based on ZeroScript architecture

Infinix is a local autonomous AI agent for Windows and Linux, controlled through supported browser-based AI chats. Its local bridge provides endpoint diagnostics, workspace tools, browser automation, shell access under a selectable capability profile, and hierarchical multi-agent delegation. No separate model API key is required for browser providers.

## 📢 About This Project

This project was created by Moonyeep using Manus AI , built upon the ZeroScript architecture. The original creator has abandoned this project and is releasing it as an open-source base for the community.

Why release this?

- The project works but needs significant improvements

- Looking for capable developers to take this base and make it better

- Fork it, modify it, rebuild it - do whatever you want

- Only requirement: Your derivative work must remain FREE and OPEN-SOURCE (GPL-3.0)

- No commercial use without keeping it open-source

Roblox Studio is an optional integration. When enabled, Infinix can also control Studio through its MCP server; the general local agent does not require Roblox Studio.

Eight AI providers are supported: DeepSeek (chat.deepseek.com, recommended), ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), Google Gemini (gemini.google.com), Kimi (kimi.ai, Moonshot AI), GLM (chat.z.ai, Z.ai), Qwen (chat.qwen.ai), Arena (arena.ai, a multi-model playground) and Meta AI (meta.ai). On ChatGPT, screenshots and image input are turned off on purpose: the free tier limits files and images on a separate quota from messages, so vision would only work part of the day. Gemini and Kimi can be unstable: Gemini tends to stop using the Roblox tools in long sessions, and Kimi sometimes uses its own native tools instead of the Roblox commands. On Arena, use Direct mode (Infinix only supports Direct; it blocks Start in Battle / Side-by-Side / Agent modes). DeepSeek is the recommended provider.

> 💬 Discord community: Join here for help and discussions.

> Also known as: Free Claude Code alternative, Free Codex alternative, OpenClaw without API key, Infinix Roblox, Infinix free download, Roblox ChatGPT agent, Roblox DeepSeek agent, Roblox Gemini agent, Roblox Kimi agent, Roblox GLM agent, Roblox Qwen agent, Roblox Arena agent, Roblox Meta AI agent, Roblox Studio AI automation, Luau AI, MCP Roblox, lemonade alternative free, lemonade.gg alternative, free Roblox AI agent, free lemonade roblox alternative

## ⚠️ Infinix is Free Beware of Paid Copycats

Infinix is 100% free and open-source. It always has been, and it always will be. There is no official paid version, no subscription, and no sign-in required to use the extension.

If you come across a site or extension using the Infinix name that asks for payment or account creation, it is not this project. The only official links are the ones listed at the top of this README.

## How it works

AI chat in browser <-> Infinix Extension <-> local Bridge -> endpoint/workspace tools and optional MCP integrations (including Roblox Studio)

The extension runs inside a supported chat page and connects to the local bridge on the same PC. The bridge provides enabled local diagnostics, workspace and process tools; the extension provides browser automation. Roblox Studio is optional and its tools appear only when that integration is enabled.

## Multi-agent teams

The supervisor can delegate bounded tasks to providers authorized at startup. Each worker runs in an inactive tab in a minimized dedicated Infinix team window with a separate per-tab ToolRegistry, so provider pages do not take focus or remain visibly open. Workers use the Basic profile and read-only diagnostics/workspace tools, including source search and Git inspection; they do not inherit terminal access, browser control, file writes, remediation, or the supervisor's Amplo permissions. Delegating children requires explicit allow_children and is bounded by the session concurrency setting and a three-level depth limit. Spawn slots are reserved before asynchronous tab creation, preventing parallel requests from exceeding the configured limit. Worker startup can take up to two minutes before a handshake timeout, and status remains starting until the provider is ready. Tool results are returned through the same result envelope as other extension tools so the supervisor receives the assigned task ID, rather than an empty {} response. Supervisor/worker messages are routed through the local bridge with direct-parent/child checks; message retries are idempotent only when the original sender and content match. agent.team.status preserves its direct-child response by default and can optionally return include_descendants=true with a bounded hierarchy and state counts. Hidden tabs continue to run where the browser allows it, but browser or OS suspension can pause them.

Reliability requirements for slow provider startup, hidden-tab execution and bridge-mediated team messaging are tracked in MULTIAGENT_RELIABILITY_REQUIREMENTS.md ; some items still require implementation.

## Software development workflow

For repository work, the local agent can load root AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md guidance and common project manifests with workspace.context , search literal source text with workspace.search , and inspect local changes using git.status and bounded git.diff . File reads support bounded line ranges. The recommended flow is to inspect repository guidance and existing changes first, search call sites before editing, make focused changes, add targeted tests, run relevant checks, and review the resulting diff. These additions provide repository context and code navigation; worker agents remain read-only and should return findings/evidence to the supervisor.

Core regression tests: python3 -m unittest discover -q . Extension tests: run node over each zeroscript-extension/test-*.js file from the repository root.

## Reusable skills

The package includes 12 task skills for endpoint diagnostics, incident response, browser automation, software development, testing, study, secure downloads, Linux privileged operations, research, data analysis, administrative assistance and multi-agent delegation. See skills/INDEX.md . The agent should load only the relevant skill and references; these guides do not grant permissions or override the active profile.

## Setup

Linux is supported with Chrome/Chromium or Edge and the start_agent.sh launcher. The launcher automatically prepares Python dependencies; see INSTALL_LINUX.md.

On Linux, the Amplo session can use the terminal.run_as_admin tool when sudo is available. If needed, the OS desktop opens its askpass authentication dialog. Enter the password there—not in the chat. It is passed directly to sudo, never to the model or Infinix logs, and is not stored by Infinix; the system may cache sudo authorization until its normal timeout.

📺 Setup tutorial on YouTube covers every step below.

### 1. Download the zip and install the extension

Download the latest zip from the Releases page and extract it. The zip contains both the Bridge and the extension folder.

On Linux, Chrome/Chromium and Edge are supported. To load the extension:

- Go to edge://extensions (Edge) or chrome://extensions (Chrome)

- Enable Developer mode (top right toggle)

- Click Load unpacked

- Select the zeroscript-extension folder from the extracted zip

### 2. (Optional) Connect Roblox Studio

Open Studio and load a Place, then enable MCP (first time only):

- Click Assistant AI in the top bar

- Click ... (top right of the Assistant panel)

- Click Manage MCP Servers

- Click Enable Studio as MCP Server

Not sure where to find these options? The video tutorial shows exactly where to click.

### 3. Run the Bridge

Windows: double-click start.bat inside the extracted folder.

macOS: double-click MacOS_Start.command inside the extracted folder. The first time, macOS will show a security warning ("could not verify... free of malware") - this is normal for any script downloaded outside the App Store, click Done, then go to System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom, and click Open Anyway. You only need to do this once.

Linux: open a terminal in the extracted project folder and run chmod +x start_agent.sh (if needed), then ./start_agent.sh . It creates a local virtual environment, installs websockets, and downloads Python 3.12 into your user directories if the system only has an older Python (e.g. Ubuntu 20.04). It does not use sudo or change system packages. See INSTALL_LINUX.md.

Keep the terminal/window open while using Infinix. The General Agent does not require Roblox Studio; enable the Studio MCP server only when you want Roblox-specific tools.

### 4. Start a session

Go to https://chat.deepseek.com (recommended), https://chatgpt.com , https://gemini.google.com , https://www.kimi.ai , https://chat.z.ai , https://chat.qwen.ai , https://arena.ai or https://www.meta.ai and open a new chat. The Infinix bar appears above the input box. Click Start session. Type what you want to build.

Only works on chat.deepseek.com, chatgpt.com, gemini.google.com, kimi.ai, chat.z.ai, chat.qwen.ai, arena.ai and meta.ai - it will not work on any other site. On Arena, keep the mode dropdown on Direct - Infinix blocks Start in Battle / Side-by-Side / Agent modes (it only drives a single Direct reply). Gemini and Kimi can be unstable (model behavior, not the extension): Gemini may stop using the Roblox tools after a while, and Kimi may use its own native tools instead. If the AI starts answering in plain text instead of acting, remind it to use the commands or start a new session.

### 5. Watch the setup tutorial

Watch the setup tutorial on YouTube

- Run Luau code directly in Studio

### The CLI-first AI coding agent runtime.

Pipe it, schedule it, embed it. One binary, any model, MCP-native — built for autonomous work, not just chat.

Website · Docs · Tap Registry · Benchmarks · Issues

Octomind is a CLI-first AI coding agent runtime. It gives an LLM real access to your repo — reading and writing files, running shells, searching code, delegating to sub-agents — through MCP tools. The same session engine works interactively , piped through stdin , as a background daemon , over WebSocket , or as an ACP sub-agent inside another agent's stack.

# Interactive octomind run developer:general # Piped — CI, scripts, automation echo " Explain the auth module " | octomind run developer:general --format plain # Daemon — keep it alive, talk to it from another terminal echo " watch the build " | octomind run --name watcher --daemon --format jsonl octomind send --name watcher " run the test suite "

## Why Octomind?

Most coding agents assume a human is watching the screen. Octomind is built for the work that keeps going after you leave.

- Policy as code, not approval popups. Deterministic guardrails — pre-call guards, post-result hooks, post-turn validators — live in TOML and scripts, so they work in CI, daemons, and scheduled runs.

- Proven on real PRs. It solved 24 of 25 held-out tasks at lower cost than the closest competitor. See the benchmarks .

- Ready-made specialists. octomind run developer:general pulls a packaged agent (prompt, model, MCP servers, tool permissions) from a tap . Publish your own with one repo.

- Sessions that stay sharp. Adaptive compression keeps long tasks moving while retaining task knowledge and the live exchange.

- Any model, any budget. Use Octomind Cloud or your own key (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Ollama, and more), pick a model per role, and set spend thresholds per request and per session. A request over its threshold stops; at the session threshold a terminal session asks y/N before continuing, while a non-interactive octomind run stops with exit code 75.

- One config. Models, tools, roles, guardrails, budgets: all TOML, no framework code.

## Quick Start

1. Install (macOS, Linux):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muvon/octomind/master/install.sh | bash

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / muvon / octomind / master / install.ps1 | iex

On macOS, you can also install with Homebrew:

brew install muvon/tap/octomind

2. Get model access. The fastest path is Octomind Cloud, which includes models and needs no configuration:

octomind login

Prefer your own provider key? Skip login and export one (also OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY ), then follow Model access to point the config at it:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY= " your_key "

3. Run a specialist in your project:

cd ~ /your/project octomind run developer:general

You're now in a session with an agent that can read your code, run commands, and edit files. The interface is a plain line prompt with markdown rendering — no TUI to learn, so it works over SSH, in tmux , and in CI logs. The first time you run a specialist, it may install its tools and ask for credentials.

> developer:general comes from the default tap muvon/tap , not your local config. Plain octomind run starts the config's default role, assistant:concierge .

Try the recorded bug-fix demo : two failing tests, an agent fix, and an independent test rerun.

## Benchmarks

Measured on octobench against 25 tasks harvested from merged pull requests across Python, PHP, Rust, C++, and JavaScript. Each agent works in the pre-fix repo; held-out tests from the merged fix decide pass or fail. These are the published July 30, 2026 results, not a measurement of this checkout.

- The harness matters. opencode used the same model and endpoint; octomind solved 24 vs 19 at roughly half the cost. All four agents ran stock invocations with no tuning, so this measures the whole harness, not individual features.

- Worst-case pricing, still ahead. glm-5.2 ran without prompt caching while Opus billed ~97% of context re-reads at cache rates — and octomind still led on solves, cost, and wall time.

- Reproducible. Per-case table, artifacts, and reproduction guide: BENCHMARK.md . Background: blog post .

## Guardrails: Policy as Code

Drop a .agents/guardrails.toml in your repo. The runtime enforces it deterministically, with no code to compile and no plugin to install.

# Pre-call deny — block a class of calls before they execute [[ guard ]] match = " shell(command=^rm \\ s+-rf?) " message = " rm -rf blocked. " # Conditional rule — only fires after the agent ran git status this session [[ guard ]] match = " shell(command=git push) " when = [ " +shell(command=git status) " ] message = " Review changes before pushing. "

Hook and validator script examples: Guardrails guide .

## Five Ways to Run It

The same session engine, exposed however your workflow needs it.

Need machine-readable results? Pass --schema schema.json to constrain the final response to a JSON Schema (requires a model with structured-output support). See Structured output .

## Features

### Specialists

octomind run developer:general # general dev, language skills auto-activate octomind run doctor:blood # blood-test interpretation specialist octomind run lawyer:sg # legal specialist

Running a specialist fetches its manifest from the tap registry, installs any required binaries, resolves credentials, starts the right MCP servers, and then opens the session.

Build and register your own:

octomind tap init yourteam/my-tap # scaffold, validate, git-init, and register locally octomind tap yourteam/my-tap # on another machine, after publishing to GitHub

The octomind- prefix is added automatically: yourteam/my-tap maps to the repository yourteam/octomind-my-tap .

## Installation

The install script detects your OS and architecture (Linux and macOS on x86_64/aarch64) and installs to ~/.local/bin/ . Pass --install-dir <DIR> or set OCTOMIND_INSTALL_DIR to override. On Windows (x86_64/aarch64), install.ps1 installs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\octomind\bin and adds it to your user PATH ; it honors OCTOMIND_INSTALL_DIR and OCTOMIND_VERSION too. install.sh still works from Git Bash or MSYS2.

Command not found? Add the install directory to your PATH :

export PATH= " $HOME /.local/bin: $PATH "

Building from source requires protoc ; see Building from source for per-OS prerequisites.

Verify:

octomind --version octomind config # generate the default config octomind run # start your first session

Shell completions: octomind completion <bash|zsh|fish|elvish|powershell> .

### Model access

Octomind Cloud — octomind login (device-code sign-in, like gh auth login ) stores a gateway key locally. The default config already uses octohub:auto . Learn more .

Bring your own key — set the provider's environment variable ( OPENROUTER_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY , …) and point the model tables at it. The supervisor and compression profiles also default to octohub:auto , so update all three:

[ model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash " [ supervisor . model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash " [ compression . model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash "

Provider details and per-role overrides: Providers & models .

## Configuration

Config lives at ~/.local/share/octomind/config/config.toml on macOS and Linux, and under %LOCALAPPDATA%/octomind/config/ on Windows. Set OCTOMIND_DATA_DIR to override the data root.

octomind config --show # view current config octomind config --validate # validate config

Override any value for a single run with -c :

octomind run -c supervisor.enabled=false

Full reference: Configuration reference · Environment variables .

### Session commands

Full list: Session commands .

### Telemetry

Octomind reports anonymous usage: which commands, tools, and models are used, plus timings, token counts, and error kinds. It never sends your code, prompts, file paths, tool arguments, or environment values. Opt out in any of three ways:

export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 # the cross-tool standard, honored first export OCTOMIND_TELEMETRY=0 # for subsequent commands in this shell # or set `telemetry = false` in config.toml

Exact field list: Telemetry .

## Documentation

Full index: doc/README.md · Hosted: octomind.run/docs .

## Contributing

The most impactful contribution isn't code — it's specialist agents. A cardiologist publishing doctor:medications . A tax attorney publishing lawyer:us . A security researcher publishing security:owasp . One TOML file, and everyone facing that problem gets a specialist-grade AI.

- How to write a tap agent

- Open issues

Code contributions are welcome too. Set up the hooks and run the gate before you push:

pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install make dev # fmt + clippy + test

Commits follow Conventional Commits . Full guide, architecture overview, and code conventions: CONTRIBUTING.md · internals: Architecture .

Community participation follows our Code of Conduct . Report vulnerabilities privately using the security policy .

# UniiChat

▶ Watch the announcement video

This repo is vibe-coded. AI agents wrote nearly all of it, and AI agents reviewed it. Read it, run it and fork it as such: expect bugs.

UniiChat runs a small team of AI agents, the uniis, on a computer you own. You talk to one of them, root. Each unii has one chat that never ends: you talk to the same agent for days, weeks, years, and it remembers. There is no hosted version: you run it yourself, on your own Claude subscription or API keys.

## How it works

- One chat, a memory tree. Every message is summarized into one line, and neighboring lines are merged in pairs, again and again, into a binary tree. Each call sees a view of the whole chat, up to 128 KB: recent messages one line each, older ones covered by fewer, broader lines. Detail fades with age, but nothing is lost.

- Zoom. A unii can open any line into the two it was made from, down to the original message. Its context never rots, and it never needs a compaction that throws the past away.

- Built in the background. Summaries are written as messages arrive. The view changes only at its end, so each call reads most of its input from the vendor's prompt cache.

- A tree of uniis. Root can spawn children, each owning one lasting part of your work (a project, your calendar, your infra), and they can spawn their own. A unii talks only to its parent and its children, by message; a message wakes it, and its turn ends in a reply it keeps for itself. Each works in its own git worktree, and a parent reviews and merges its children's branches. Uniis ask before spawning: nothing grows without your OK.

- Every window is a view. One process, the hub, keeps every chat. A browser tab or a terminal shows them live: the browser lists the uniis as a tree at the left; in the terminal, Tab cycles through them and /tab <name> opens one.

The design is in the header comment of each file. Start with Memory.ts (the tree and the view), Server.ts (the hub) and AskAI.ts (model calls and the cache).

## Run it

You need Bun , git, and Claude Code signed in to your Claude subscription:

git clone https://github.com/VictorTaelin/uniichat cd uniichat bun install claude # sign in, then quit mkdir -p ~/t/unii/root && cd ~/t/unii/root git init && git commit --allow-empty -m root # root's worktree cd - && bun Server.ts # the hub, on http://127.0.0.1:8788

Root works in that repo; each child works in a worktree of it beside it, ~/t/unii/<name> , on a branch of its own. Then, in another terminal:

bun Term.ts # a terminal view

or open the browser view, signed in by the hub's key ( bun Term.ts link prints the same link):

open "http://127.0.0.1:8788/auth?key=$(cat ~/.opt/key)"

The key, ~/.opt/key , is made at the first start; whoever has it reaches every unii and every command they run, so keep it private.

Every unii's chat is a dir chat/<name>/ of the hub's own worktree, ~/t/unii/.chats (branch chats , checked out at chat/ only): one JSON line per message (main/), summary (tree/) and thought (mind/). Only the hub writes them; at the end of each turn it commits that unii's chat, and merges chats into root's branch while root sleeps. They are the memory: back the repo up.

## From your phone, or anywhere

The hub listens only on 127.0.0.1. Run it on a machine that stays on, and reach it over a private network, never the open internet. With Tailscale :

tailscale serve --bg 8788

serves it over HTTPS, at your machine's Tailscale name, to your own computers and phone only. Set site (below) to that address, and open <site>/auth?key=<key> once in each browser.

To let the uniis run commands on another computer (their mac tool), link it to the hub's socket, ~/.opt/mac.sock , with ssh -W : the hub sends {"$":"job","id","unii","command"} and {"$":"stop","id"} , one JSON object a line, and the computer answers each job once with {"$":"out","id","text","code"} (Server.ts says more). Closing the link ends their access.

## Config

~/.opt/config.json (optional). Each key may also be set as the variable OPT_<KEY> :

- root : root's worktree, a git checkout you make (default ~/t/unii/root ). A child's worktree is beside it, ~/t/unii/<name> , on branch <name> , and so is the hub's, .chats .

- chats : the chats' dir in the repo (default chat ).

- site : the address you open it at (default http://127.0.0.1:8788 ).

- vendors : what the uniis may run on, comma-separated: claude-sub (your subscription, through the claude CLI; the default), claude-api ( ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ), openai-api ( OPENAI_API_KEY ).

- models : the models offered: opus-5.5 , gpt-6-astra .

- pick : what a unii runs on until you pick another, vendor:model:effort:speed (default claude-sub:opus-5.5:high:slow ).

- compactor : what writes the summaries (default the same).

- accounts : a dir of claude_<id>.token files, each a token from claude setup-token , used in order: when one reaches its limit, the next. None: the CLI's own login.

- rules : a file appended to every system prompt: who you are, how your files are organized, how you want work done.

- computer : 1 lets the uniis use the screen, mouse and keyboard of the Mac the hub runs on (it compiles Computer.swift with swiftc; macOS asks for Screen Recording and Accessibility).

API keys come from the environment, read at start and removed from it, so no command a unii runs inherits them: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY .

Other commands:

bun test # the tests

The hub builds the site's script from web/src as it starts.

Showcase · Weights (Hugging Face) · ComfyUI nodes · GGUF setup guide · 8-step LoRA for full-size MiniMax-H3

- stream is only ~2% slower than none on the same GPU.

All runs are end-to-end at 1344×768 and 6 steps : text encoding, transformer, and video and audio VAE decode. Each a / b cell is total time for a 5.2 s / 15 s clip (124 / 362 frames).

### Consumer RTX GPUs: t2va

- GGUF setup: ComfyUI, Q4_K_M , and the 15.7 GB nvfp4 text encoder. 32 GB and 16 GB PCs use --fast-disk with models on NVMe ( Host RAM ). Peak RSS is 34–37 GiB on ≥ 64 GB PCs. Anonymous RSS is ~8–16 GiB on 32 GB PCs and ~8 GiB on 16 GB PCs.

- INT8 setup: hyperflow-h3-flash --offload stream . It needs ≥ 91 GiB of system RAM with the bf16 text encoder, or ~69 GiB with fp8 . The 15 s RTX 5090 run used fp8 .

- The INT8 transformer is 10–20% faster. GGUF needs less than half the system RAM. The transformer takes over 80% of the time and is compute bound. ComfyUI dequantizes Q4_K_M weights at run time.

- Use --fast-disk on 16 GB and 32 GB PCs. It streams unresident weights from the OS file page cache. Without it, ComfyUI-GGUF copies the 9 GB transformer into pinned RAM when VRAM overflows. 16 GB PCs then run out of RAM on 15 s clips. On 32 GB PCs, the RTX 3090 and 5090 become 13% and 21% slower (text encoding takes 27–31 s instead of 7–9 s).

- 32 GB of VRAM holds both models. On the RTX 5090, the text encoder and transformer stay in VRAM together (0.8 s text encoding). On 24 GB GPUs, ComfyUI swaps them between stages (10–16 s text encoding).

- Keyframe tasks ( i2v , flf2v ): See GGUF guide: Performance .

### Consumer RTX GPUs: ref2va

- References: Two 768p stills generated with t2va (a person and a street market). Mixed is one still, one 5.2 s reference video with its soundtrack, and one audio clip.

- INT8 setup: 100–125 GB of system RAM (80–88 GiB process RSS). ¹ On 24 GB GPUs, 15 s mixed runs need --block-chunk 16384 . Without it, they run out of VRAM.

- GGUF setup: ComfyUI on ≥ 64 GB RAM, with hyperflow_ref2v_api.json and the nvfp4 text encoder. ref_image_size match (default) downscales each reference to the output's pixel area and keeps its aspect ratio. max downscales only above a 2048 short edge. The max runs used the stills upscaled to 3584×2048, the size the INT8 pipeline uses. ² max at 15 s needs python main.py --disable-cuda-malloc . The default cudaMallocAsync allocator fails with CUDA error: invalid argument .

- Each reference adds tokens to every step. At a 2048 short edge, one image adds ~14,300 tokens (about seven 768p latent frames). The clip itself is 37,710 tokens at 5.2 s and 109,062 at 15 s. Attention cost grows with the square of the token count. So at 5.2 s, the INT8 transformer takes 2.6–2.9× its t2va time with two images and 5.2–5.8× with the mixed set.

- GGUF match is the fastest image-reference path. It adds 24–36% to t2v at 5.2 s and 7–15% at 15 s. At the same reference size ( max ), GGUF is 11–25% slower than INT8 at 5.2 s and 8–9% slower at 15 s.

- --fast-disk also works for ref2v . 32 GB and 16 GB PCs ran 5.2 s and 15 s clips on all three GPUs, within 4% of ≥ 64 GB RAM at 15 s. See GGUF guide: Host RAM .

## Architecture and Hardware Notes

### How It Works

HyperFlow H3 Flash changes the MiniMax-H3 transformer in three ways:

- Structural pruning and low-rank factorization:

- Rotated W8A8 INT8 quantization ( convrot ): 180 linear layers are quantized to W8A8 INT8 behind a block-diagonal Hadamard rotation.

- Two-time (t, r) conditioning: Every token receives the current noise level t and the step endpoint r . This enables 4-to-8-step sampling without CFG. Conditioning tokens stay at their anchor noise level ( r = t ).

### Multi-GPU and Kernel Dispatch ( hyperflow-h3-flash )

- Sequence and VAE parallelism ( --gpus N ): Ulysses context parallelism splits the packed transformer sequence across $N$ GPUs. Ranks encode keyframes and references and decode spatial video VAE tiles in parallel. Then they all-gather and blend the tiles to match single-GPU output bitwise.

- Text encoder placement: With --offload none and the bf16 text encoder, FSDP2 shards the 50 GiB text encoder across GPUs. This cuts 4-GPU peak VRAM from 91 GiB to 59 GiB/GPU. When offloading or using fp8 , rank 0 runs the text encoder and broadcasts the embeddings (~2 MB).

- Reproducibility: The same seed, GPU architecture, GPU count, and attention backend produce bitwise-identical clips. text_encoder_fsdp and vae_parallel preserve bitwise output.

You have a running AI Gude. To follow your own feeds, continue with Configure Shows, Feeds and Schedules .

## Concepts

A User owns CastProfiles, and each CastProfile is a show. A CastProfile lists the Subscriptions it draws Content from, which are RSS feeds, a Max Lookback that says how old Content may be, and Schedules that say when an Episode is made. Content is one item that a Subscription delivers, such as an article. An Episode is one audio file with its Script and its Chapters, one Chapter for each Section of the Script.

The core flow, from a Schedule to a finished Episode:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant S as Scheduler participant W as Worker participant DB as Database participant R as RSS feeds participant C as Crawler participant G as Gemini participant F as ffmpeg S->>W: Schedule is due, queue the CastProfile Note over S,W: "Generate now" queues the same request W->>DB: Which Content was used by this CastProfile already? W->>R: Fetch the Subscriptions, Content within the Max Lookback R->>C: Retrieve the full text of each new article C-->>R: Cleaned text, from the cache while it is fresh R-->>W: Contents alt nothing new W-->>S: No Episode, only a log line else new Content W->>G: Rules, style guide and numbered Contents G-->>W: Script with title and Sections loop every Section W->>G: Speak the Section G-->>W: Speech as PCM end W->>F: Speech joined with a pause between Sections F-->>W: One OGG/Opus file W->>W: Write the Chapters into the file W->>DB: Save Episode, Script, Chapters, sources and usage end Note over W,DB: Any failure saves the Episode as failed, with its reason

What to keep in mind:

- One Episode is produced at a time. Requests wait in a queue.

- Choose a Max Lookback that is larger than the interval between two Schedules. Content older than the Max Lookback is never considered, so a shorter one lets articles fall through the gap between two Episodes.

- A larger Max Lookback does no harm, because each Episode remembers the Content it used and no article is told twice. Deleting an Episode gives its Content back.

- A Schedule that was due while the service was not running is made up at the start, once for each CastProfile.

- A failed Episode stays in the list with its reason. You can try again or dismiss it.

- Each Section is spoken in its own call, which makes the Chapters exact, and the audio is encoded once at the end.

Behind the steps are small interfaces, and one adapter each does the work today:

flowchart LR P["Episode production"] P --> CR["ContentRepository"] --> RSS["RSS feeds"] P --> CW["Crawler"] --> FC["Firecrawl"] P --> SW["ScriptWriter"] --> GM["Gemini text"] P --> TT["TTS"] --> GT["Gemini speech"] P --> AE["AudioEncoder"] --> FF["ffmpeg"] P --> ER["EpisodeRepository"] --> DB["SQLite"] P --> AS["AudioStore"] --> FS["Files"]

The only part you can run in two ways is the Crawler, which retrieves the full text of the articles. You choose it with the setting firecrawl_url .

- The hosted Firecrawl is the default and needs FIRECRAWL_API_KEY . There is nothing to run, and it bills per page. The Getting Started uses it.

- A Firecrawl of your own costs nothing per page. Set firecrawl_url to its address. The key is then optional and is sent only when it is set. task serve starts one in Docker from hack/firecrawl/ , but that one is for development only and has no authentication, so it is not a recipe for hosting.

AI Gude keeps crawled pages for crawl_cache_ttl , which is ten days by default, and shares them between all Users. An article that is retrieved again soon costs nothing.

### Configure the Service Settings

Settings apply to the whole service. The commented example is hack/aigude.toml .

- Settings come from built-in defaults, the settings file, environment variables and flags, and each one overrides the one before it. An environment variable is AIGUDE_ plus the upper-case key, for example AIGUDE_LISTEN_ADDR . A flag is the key with hyphens, for example --listen-addr .

- The settings file is aigude.toml in the working directory of the service, or the file given with --config . It is optional. The example lists every setting with its default and a comment, and a test guards that the defaults it shows are the real ones. Copy it and delete what you do not want to change.

- A key the service does not know is an error, and so is an invalid value. The message names the setting. Changes need a restart.

- The API keys GEMINI_API_KEY and FIRECRAWL_API_KEY are not settings. A key in the settings file is rejected as an unknown key and the service does not start, so they come from the environment only.

### Configure Shows, Feeds and Schedules

Shows, feeds and Schedules belong to a User and live in that User's file. The commented example is hack/users/demo.toml , and it is the template for new Users.

- Each User has one .toml file in the folder users_dir , which is users by default. The file name is free, and the User is identified by the Id inside.

- A file holds the User, its CastProfiles, and for each CastProfile the Subscriptions, Max Lookback, language, voice, prompt and Schedules.

- The files are followed while the service runs, so an edit takes effect without a restart. A file that turns invalid keeps the last valid setup of its User, and the interface shows the problem. A deleted file takes its User away.

- A User can edit their own file in the interface with "Edit User Config". To check files without starting anything run this:

aigude validate --users-dir users

### Configure Multiple Users and Authentication

AI Gude has no sign-in of its own. Authentication is the job of a reverse proxy in front of it. The proxy tells AI Gude who is asking in a request header, and from then on each person works in their own User and cannot reach another one.

#### Start without authentication

Without the header everyone who reaches the port can switch between all Users in the interface, produce and delete Episodes and edit every User Config. At home on a network you trust that is a fine way to share one instance. It is also why the service listens on 127.0.0.1 by default. Do not leave it like this on a network that others can reach.

To add a User, copy hack/users/demo.toml into the users folder and change the [user] table and what follows. The file is picked up at once.

#### Pin each person to their User

After the proxy has authenticated a person, it sets the header X-Aigude-User to the Id of their User. Use the Id and not the display name, because only the Id never changes.

A request with this header belongs to that User. The interface offers no switch to another User, a request to switch is refused, and the person sees only their own Episodes and edits only their own User Config. A header that is empty, that names no User or that names a User without a valid setup is answered with 403 for every request.

Two things have to hold for this to be safe:

- The port is reachable only through the proxy.

- The proxy sets the header itself on every request and never passes one on from the client. A request without the header gets full rights, so a proxy that forgets it opens the service to everyone.

#### Example with Traefik and Basic Auth

Traefik asks for a user name and a password and writes the name into X-Aigude-User . So the user name of the Basic Auth is the Id of the User. Create the users file with one line for each person, for example with htpasswd :

htpasswd -nB alex >> /etc/traefik/users

Then add the route and its middleware to the dynamic configuration of Traefik. Replace the host name and the address of the service. The example assumes an entry point websecure and a certificate resolver letsencrypt . Serve it over HTTPS, because Basic Auth sends the password with every request.

http : routers : aigude : rule : Host(`aigude.example.org`) entryPoints : - websecure service : aigude middlewares : - aigude-auth tls : certResolver : letsencrypt middlewares : aigude-auth : basicAuth : usersFile : /etc/traefik/users realm : AI Gude headerField : X-Aigude-User removeHeader : true services : aigude : loadBalancer : servers : - url : http://127.0.0.1:8080

headerField makes Traefik set X-Aigude-User from the user name and replaces a value that the client sent, and removeHeader keeps the credentials from reaching AI Gude. A name in the users file that is not a User of AI Gude is answered with 403.

#### Show the demo User to visitors

The User with the Id demo is shown in Demo Mode. Whoever looks at its pages can browse and play its Episodes, and nothing can be changed. The log and the editor of the User Config are closed, and the interface leaves out what only the person running the service should see, such as problems in the User Config files. Because "Generate now" is closed too, the Episodes of the demo User come from its Schedules. Create it like any User, for example from the sample hack/users/demo.toml with the Id demo .

### Run and Maintain the Service

- Produce an Episode with "Generate now" on a CastProfile, or let its Schedules do it.

- Episodes are deleted with their audio once they are older than the Retention, the time Episodes are kept. The setting is episode_retention , it is 30 days by default, it counts from the creation of the Episode and it applies to failed Episodes too. 0 keeps them for ever. The check runs at the start and once a day, and a deleted Episode gives its Content back.

- The meter on an Episode shows what it consumed, such as tokens and crawled pages.

- GET /healthz answers 200 with ok and checks nothing behind it, not the database, not Gemini and not Firecrawl. It needs no headers of a proxy.

The agent will:

- Study the discovered mechanisms.

- Plan the interactions between their different mechanical components.

- And finally, turn those plans into python code for Blender , that will: Create the required rigs for controlling the different mechanisms. Animate them according to plan ! 🤯

- Create the required rigs for controlling the different mechanisms.

- Animate them according to plan ! 🤯

## Installation

Note

The installation process will install every required tool and dependency locally on this project repo, in order to avoid polluting the host OS .

However, there is a requirement of setting several env vars on rc files, like e.g. .bashrc or .zshrc

The installed dependencies, like e.g. Blender, are git-ignored by default.

You'll need Python 3.12+ installed.

Start by cloning the repo and running the setup script , pick the right one for your OS:

git clone https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha.git cd ldraw-mecha ./setup-macos.sh # or ./setup-linux.sh, ./setup-win-wsl.sh

### Installed during setup

At the end of the setup process, you'll get a snippet with the env vars to be added to your shell profile ( .bashrc , .zshrc , etc.), something like e.g.:

# >>> ldraw-mecha (from setup-macos.sh) >>> export LDRAW_DIR= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw " export LDRAWDIR= " $LDRAW_DIR " export BLENDER_BIN= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender " export LEOCAD= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/LeoCAD.app/Contents/MacOS/LeoCAD " export LDRAW_XRAY_CACHE= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/.cache/ldraw-xray " export LDRAW_ANNOTATOR_DB= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw-info.db " # export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... # optional: Jev semantic search (jev-rerank) # other env vars... # <<< ldraw-mecha <<<

If you're on VS Code or a terminal , restart it in order to get an updated env with the newly added env vars.

## Usage

For inspecting and selecting one pre-annotated model to animate, open the annotated models selector by running:

python3 model-selector/serve.py

Then, take a look at the Process guide for a step-by-step usage example .

## Samples

More samples available at: Gallery

Animations have been generated from original models , not from ai-generated ones.

These are some samples of animations by different agents, take a look at their Summaries for more details.

## 42043 Mercedes-Benz Arocs flatbed truck: the pneumatic crane on its own

- Agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5

- Original model: 42043-1_Flatbed-Trailer.mpd

## Minifig movement catalog: ten minifigs, three moves each

## Agent's informational sources

## Why and How?

After publishing LDraw Nova , a sibling project for agentic generation of LDraw models , several people reached out to me asking about if models could be animated somehow.

During the development of Nova, I noticed that adding some special annotations to .mpd original model source files , and then giving those to agents , would:

- Help agents in understanding how to build other different models.

- But also, in understanding how a model was built .

Which gave me the idea that, maybe, an agent would also understand how a model would work.

### Reverse-engineering mechanisms from their sources

As a first step to it, I gave annotated models to different agents, and prompted them to infer (reverse-engineer) their constituent submodels (see Haiku 5.5. experiment below).

Results from inference experiments were both pretty good and consistent across different agents, and I also noticed the following: many of the submodels inferred were actually mechanisms.

After questioning several agents about those inferred mechanisms, regarding how would they actually work , I also got consistent results: agents would describe behaviours based on the descriptions for the parts on a mechanism! 🤯

At this point, I had the following:

- Agents would split and refine models into submodels and mechanisms.

- Agents would understand each mechanism in isolation .

- Agents would understand how individual mechanisms worked .

The result of an actual divide-and-conquer process , right? 🤓

Which would make handling individual mechanisms manageable. 🤩

### Correlating LDraw source code to a 3D model

Now, there was the matter of giving agents the means to actually animate mechanisms they already knew how they worked.

I was playing with Blender MCP at the time, and Blender looked promising as a tool that would provide agents a way to manipulate LDraw models in 3D , imported into Blender as glTF (.glb) files.

But there was still an open issue:

How to map from a refined model source code an agent would understand, to its equivalent 3D model in glTF format an agent could manipulate?

And the solution I found was:

Annotate the 3D glTF model's nodes with the same annotations as the source code, so the agent would:

- Outside Blender: plan on submodels 🤔 and parts as source code.

- Inside Blender: execute on matching nodes ✨ on the 3D glTF model.

### Putting the pieces together 😉

Now, I had a draft for a process , but no tools for the agent to use and carry it forward.

Given that the process would require a high amount of complex geometric and spatial calculations , I asked the agent to derive a new python toolset from the one created for ldraw-nova

The new python toolset I refined iteratively , by giving the agent simple models at the beginning, and increasingly complex ones each time.

And to test it, I gave an agent instructions to:

- first, plan from an annotated and refined .mpd model

- then, generate a glTF 3D version of it, with matching annotations

- then, upload it to Blender

- and then, produce the Blender python scripts that would animate the model as planned.

And it finally worked ! 🚀🚀🚀

(but not perfectly) 😜

## Experiment - Claude Haiku 5.5 reverse-engineering session

# Umbra

An autonomous agent that lives on your Android phone. Tell it what to do; it works in the background, operates apps for you, writes and builds code in a real Linux environment on the same device, checks its own work, and asks before anything risky.

- Operates the phone. It reads the screen (accessibility tree first, screenshots when needed), taps, types, scrolls, opens apps, reads notifications and logs, and verifies that each action did what it should. Work can run in an invisible background display, so you keep using the phone.

- A Linux machine in your pocket. A Debian environment (bash, git, Python, Bun, and add-on toolchains such as C/C++, Java, Node, Android app builds and a virtual desktop) where the agent builds and tests software. Files live in workspaces both worlds can see.

- Built on omp , a coding agent with a mature tool and planning loop, extended here with Android, privileged and desktop tools. Models are yours: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible server.

- You stay in control. Risky actions (payments, messages, deleting data, security settings, installing apps, passwords) always need your approval, from the app, a notification or a floating control. The agent can never operate its own app or answer its own approvals. Everything it asked and you answered is kept in a history. Settings → Stop and take back takes access back (stop everything, revoke the helpers, turn screen control off, delete the history); each of these says what it ends before it does it. The Linux side runs without privileges and cannot change its own system files or read the app's private data; the limits of that are in ADR 0010 .

- Resumable. Tasks are persistent sessions: pause, resume, stop, follow up, restart after the app or the agent crashes; terminals live in tmux and survive the app; a session may resume by itself after a restart only under a resume contract you gave it.

# AIQuota

See what's left of your AI subscriptions every time you open a terminal.

ChatGPT nearly out until 3 pm? Open Claude instead. AIQuota tells you before you start the coding agent, not halfway through a task.

- A status band when a terminal opens : one section per account, with a green, yellow or red dot showing how close it is to its limit

- In the title bar , always visible and refreshed in the background

- Your accounts, your order : only the ones you list are shown or queried

- Instant : opening a terminal never waits for the network

- Tiny and portable : one POSIX sh script that needs only awk and curl

## Install

List your accounts in the order you want them:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/francescobianco/aiquota/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --display=codex,claude,copilot,freebuff

Then open a new terminal. This installs the script to ~/.local/bin and adds one line to your shell's startup file. To change the accounts or their order, run it again; the line is replaced, not duplicated:

aiquota install --display=claude,codex

Prefer to do it by hand? Put bin/aiquota in your PATH and add this as the last line of your startup file:

## Usage

### The band

● ChatGPT Plus [5h 12% ↻1h48m] [7d 61%] ┃ ● Claude Max 5x [5h 99%] [7d 92%] ┃ ● Freebuff Free [day 100%]

- The dot is a traffic light for the account's tightest window: green from 50% left, yellow from 20%, red below that. Grey means no data, for example after a login expires.

- [5h 12%] is one window and the share left. An account can have several.

- ↻1h48m is the time until that window resets, shown when less than half is left.

An empty line separates the band from your first prompt. To remove it, add --no-blank-line to aiquota install or to your startup line.

The band always stays on one row. On narrower terminals it gives up detail in this order:

It uses 256 colors where available and falls back to 16 colors and plain ASCII.

### Short names

Add --short-names to aiquota install or to your startup line to always use short names in the band and the title:

● GPT Plus [5h 12% ↻1h48m] [7d 61%] ┃ ● Cld Max 5x [5h 99%] [7d 92%] ┃ ● Fbf Free [day 100%]

The full aiquota view keeps the complete names.

### The title bar

Title bars only show plain text, so this is a shorter summary with no colors or plan names:

ChatGPT 12% 1h48m │ Claude 92% │ Freebuff 100%

For each account you get the share left in the window that will stop you first. The time until it resets appears when less than half is left.

A ~ before a value means it may be out of date: the login expired, the network failed, or the window has reset since the last successful check.

To use it in a tmux status bar:

set -g status-right ' #(aiquota line --plain --display=codex,claude) '

## Accounts

Note

These are mostly undocumented endpoints , the same ones the agents use for their own usage screens. They can change without notice. When one does, AIQuota keeps showing the last known values, marked ~ .

### Flat subscriptions only

This is a deliberate limit, not a missing feature. AIQuota answers one question: which of the agents I already pay for can I still use right now? That means quota measured in time and resources until the next reset. API keys and metered, usage-based plans are never queried or shown, even if they are on your machine.

## Good to know

Logins expire while you're away. AIQuota reads each agent's credentials but never refreshes them, because refresh tokens can rotate and using one could log you out of the agent. So after a long break an account may show login expired , or its last known values marked ~ , until you next open that agent. For example, the Claude access token lasts for hours and the ChatGPT one for days.

It replaces your title. If your title bar normally shows the current directory, that's what you give up. Set AIQUOTA_TITLE=0 before the startup line to keep your title and only get the band when a terminal opens.

IDE terminals show the band, not the title. The band appears each time a terminal opens, in any terminal. JetBrains IDEs use their own fixed tab names, so the title summary doesn't appear there. In VS Code, set "terminal.integrated.tabs.title": "${sequence}" to see it in the tab. In either IDE, run aiquota for the full view.

Gemini is limited by Google. Since June 2026, Gemini CLI login has only been served for Standard and Enterprise seats, so personal accounts show no flat subscription found .

## Settings

Set these as environment variables before the startup line, or in ~/.config/aiquota/config :

## Privacy and security

AIQuota has no server and no telemetry. Each token goes only to the service that issued it.

- Credentials are read-only, and are never copied to the cache or passed on a command line.

- The cache in ~/.cache/aiquota holds only plan names, percentages and times, and only you can read it.

- Text from the network is stripped of control characters before it can reach your terminal.

- Redirects are not followed, so a token can't be forwarded to another host.

## Compatibility

Runs anywhere with a POSIX shell, awk and curl .

## Contributing

New accounts are welcome as long as they are flat subscriptions. See CONTRIBUTING.md .

# RigHaven

RigHaven is a home and an on-demand toolbox for AI agents. You describe an objective; a coordinator composes a team of roles for it, picks the skills and the tools they need (99 managed CLI tools, from documents and video to CAD, data and networks), runs each role in its own isolated container and follows the work through review and delivery. You decide at every step : tool alternatives come with their trade-offs, each phase waits for your reply, and the runtime, not the model's goodwill, enforces your policies before anything is delivered.

15-second teaser ( MP4 ), produced by RigHaven itself: an EffectCraft motion-graphics role and a SoundCraft sound role working from the brief “a teaser explaining RigHaven's architecture”. It is promotional material; the guarantees RigHaven actually enforces are described below.

## What you can do with it

How tasks, recipes, teams, skills, environments, connections and policies fit together: Concepts .

## Quick start

### 1. Install: choose one

The first start downloads the verified images (about 1 GB, once).

### 2. Sign in and connect a model

- Create the first account: it becomes the administrator . Later accounts are ordinary users (if the administrator enables registration).

- Open Models & resources and connect at least one provider: OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Kimi, OpenRouter…). Choose the model of the coordinator and of the team. See model providers .

### 3. Your first task

- Press New task and write what you want, for example: "A two-page PDF report comparing the three CSV files I attach, with one chart per file; keep the editable sources." Attach the files.

- Answer the coordinator's questions and choose among the tool alternatives it proposes. There is no team to create and nothing to install first: the environment is prepared on demand.

- Follow the task card above the chat: the goal, the progress, the decision waiting for you. Each phase shows its result and waits for your reply.

- Open the delivered files and their sources, then accept or ask for a focused revision.

Next: try a Recipe (Recipes → Use this recipe ), add a Connection to a database, or change the language in Account & preferences → Appearance .

## Connect your PC, your phone and your machines

When RigHaven runs on a server, it cannot see your desk. Three small pieces bring it there; all of them connect to the server, so no router port is opened:

RigHaven can also be installed from the browser as an app, with a one-line task card on small screens: phones and the installable app .

## How a project runs

flowchart LR Brief[Brief with you] --> Choice{Tool alternatives?} Choice -- pros, cons, recommendation --> User[You choose] Choice -- none --> Plans User --> Plans[Execution plan + policy plan] Plans --> Phases[Phases: roles in isolated environments] Phases --> Review[Independent review] Review --> Decision{Your decision} Decision -- changes --> Phases Decision -- approve --> Validation[Policy validation of the finished product] Validation --> Delivery[Delivery with editable sources]

- Isolated roles. Each assignment runs in its own container, with all capabilities dropped and resource limits; it reads the project read-only and writes only its own staging folder. Other roles see only what it deliberately publishes. Several environments can work in parallel within the configured CPU/RAM.

- Environments on demand. The software a task needs is installed into a reusable image, at the versions you choose; an environment can be kept ready for recurring work.

- Your approvals. Writes to devices and databases, vulnerability scans and phase results wait for you; an approved action runs once, exactly as approved.

- Network egress. With RIGHAVEN_WORKER_EGRESS=allowlist each job reaches only its model provider and the domains its role declares, and every blocked connection is reported.

## Personal work and shared infrastructure

Administrators manage accounts ( User administration ), shared connections, default program versions, capacity and software-image imports. Maintenance & reset removes selected conversations, profiles or overrides after a typed confirmation. Details: Workspace guide .

git clone https://github.com/ggmm82/righaven.git cd righaven cp .env.example .env

Set a unique RIGHAVEN_PASSWORD of at least 16 characters in .env , then:

bash righaven.sh up

Open http://localhost:2026 . The local proxy first asks for RIGHAVEN_USER and RIGHAVEN_PASSWORD (a gate, not an application account); then create or sign in to your RigHaven account.

English is the default interface language; Italian is available.

# team-solve

A multi-agent harness for programming problems, written as a Memdoor workflow. Five roles (planner, two ideators, solver, manager) and a repair worker each start from a fresh context and talk only through files on disk. A shell script that runs the samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of GVS5H (Lee, 2026: five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard).

Rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts on Qwen3.8-27B, their loop scored a mean of 9.8 of 10 over five passes on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, against 9.6 for their own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone ( below , every run published).

The coder wrote these files itself from a description of the method (2026-10-25). Nobody hand-wrote them.

## Five passes on the authors' ten (2026-10-31)

GVS5H's own harness, rebuilt as a Memdoor workflow on the same model: Qwen3.8-27B, a 128K reply cap, the authors' prompts and loop. The first ten problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes, every program graded on every public and hidden test with their corrected grader.

The authors' columns are their repository's regraded result files ( q38_multiagent_pN , fable5_single_pN ), the numbers in their paper. bench/results/parity-5pass/ holds all 50 runs: every request and reply, the program, the grader's full output, each call's cost and the host that served it, and every attempt that did not count. 49 of 50 solved; the 50 runs cost $35.79 (15.3M output tokens), $38.77 with the 16 attempts that were cut by a clock, stopped for a fix or paused.

Note: ten problems, five passes each, not the authors' 100. The contests date from 29 March to 6 April 2025, and the model may have seen them in training: contamination cannot be ruled out. Fable 5's column is a single call per problem from the authors' files; it was not run in this harness. The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests. A run took a median of 40 minutes of model time (the longest 4 hours) and $0.39. All on OpenRouter, not a local machine; Modal does not publish its precision. Local paths in the run scripts and in four tracebacks a manager was shown read <scratch> and $HOME ; nothing else in the runs is edited.

Same as the authors'. Every message, byte for byte: lib/test_parity.py runs their multiagent_solve and our workflow against one scripted model and compares each request (four cases, all identical; a one-character change makes them differ). The temperatures (plan 0.3, ideation 0.4, manager and worker 0.2), top_p 0.95 and top_k 20 (what their vLLM applied from the model's own config), the 128K cap, up to 10 rounds, a cut-off worker summarized, and a reply with no text answered by its reasoning.

Different. The host. Theirs was their own vLLM in FP8. Ours is OpenRouter, asked in the order Modal, CoreWeave, Parasail, Wafer until Modal slowed to 14 tokens/s, then the FP8 hosts only (Wafer, Parasail, CoreWeave): 203 calls were served by Modal, 27 by CoreWeave and 115 by Wafer, every one of the FP8 order's calls by Wafer. Three runs were moved mid-run, their finished steps kept ( log/host-switch.txt ).

What it took. The problem text was the mismatch: our first version wrote its own task file around each problem, and the 27B planned worse from it than from the authors' exact LiveCodeBench text (arc196_c's plan: 0 of 2 against 2 of 2). Four Memdoor changes let a workflow ask what their harness asks: a task answers with the model's reasoning when it wrote no text, top_p / top_k on a model line, mark_cutoff for a reply cut at the cap, and a call that runs on its own four-hour clock.

Where it lost. Twice, the same two gaps in the authors' loop:

- Pass 5, abc399_e (32 of 44 hidden): round 1's program was right; the manager invented a counterexample with a wrong expected answer, the team rewrote it, and the new program passed the samples, which do not cover the case.

- Pass 4, arc196_c and arc196_d: a program passing every hidden test was overwritten by a later round because the manager did not say done; both got a correct program back before the loop's end (arc196_d at round 8, arc196_c through the final call), at $3.44 and $4.24, the two most expensive runs.

Both are fixable without changing the method (check a manager's counterexample against a brute force on small inputs; keep the last program that passed the samples). Neither is in these numbers.

## Run it

curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash memdoor connect openrouter # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor mkdir -p ~/.memdoor/workflows cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/ # the library: any project sees it mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* . # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait # progress on stderr, exit 0 when every sample passes

/workflow in memdoor tui draws the same run live. For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in / tests/N.out files beside it. The program is solution.py , read from stdin, compared to the samples with diff . It needs Python 3 and bash. To keep it with one repo instead, copy the folder into that project's .memdoor/workflows/ . The project's copy wins.

The steps name no model. Whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one included ( memdoor connect local for janis, Ollama or llama-server).

## How it works

# bootgpt

A neural network that boots your PC.

The MBR is 512 bytes of hand written asm. It loads an 11.5 KB int8 model from the next 23 sectors and runs it in 16-bit real mode on a 386. No OS, no C runtime, nothing. The machine wakes up and dreams a Linux boot log: timestamps, PCI bars, ACPI events for hardware that never existed.

Build thread: https://x.com/krlntn/status/2116514628457185757

With 8 chars of context and one hidden layer this is roughly the quality you get:

[ 2.283888] pci 0000:01:01.4: [1b36:0a35] ryndrde c4128 6422 Vveine [ 1.953886] pci 0000:01:1f.2: reg 0x10: [mem 0x7e4515e5-0x2d766c27] usbbore: reg [ 0.206596] Command line: BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinu -5.5.2-1-generic gcc version 13.3.0, GNU ld ... [ 1.815765] ACPI: PCI Interrupt Link [LNKA: v/s.xos212 [ 1.883084] NET: Registered protocol family 16

## Run it

brew install nasm qemu python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install numpy ./build.sh ./run.sh

disk.img is a normal boot image. dd it to a USB stick and boot any BIOS box if you have one. It only reads its own sectors.

## Pieces

corpus_gen.py makes 3 MB of fake dmesg. One kernel version and one disk per boot session, because real boot logs repeat themselves and that repetition is what makes a tiny model look sane.

train.py trains the model (char embeddings, one hidden layer, softmax) and quantizes everything to int8 with power-of-two scales, so the boot sector can do the whole forward pass with imul and a single idiv. The script also simulates the exact integer math the asm will run, LCG sampler included, so the Python output and the boot sector output can be diffed. They match char for char.

boot.asm is the entire runtime: int 13h to load weights, int 10h to print, a softclip activation done with cdq/idiv, argmax sampling with timer seeded noise. Any keypress reboots the machine.

record.py records the demo gif from headless QEMU through the monitor socket. No window involved.

The boot sector is code only. Strings, weights and the vocab table all live in the data sectors, it was the only way to fit inference plus BIOS plumbing into 510 bytes.

## Prior art

The boot sector genre is old and glorious. Oscar Toledo put chess , a whole OS and even a BASIC interpreter in there, other people did a C compiler , all inside 512 bytes. His book on boot sector games is a good read.

The closest neighbor is sectorllm , which boots a real llama2 transformer (5 layers, attention, the works) from about 1.2 KB of real mode asm, running Karpathy's stories260K model. sectorlisp-nn runs a TensorFlow-trained network during boot on a Lisp interpreter, and there are UEFI apps that boot straight into llama-class models on modern hardware.

bootgpt takes the other extreme: the whole engine fits in the 510-byte MBR itself, weights and strings live in the following sectors, and the model is not a general story teller but a tiny char-level net trained for exactly one thing, hallucinating the boot log of the machine it wakes up on.

## The Problem

Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides.

### How Context Mode Solves It

Context Mode is an MCP server that solves all four sides of this problem:

- Context Saving — Sandbox tools keep raw data out of the context window. 315 KB becomes 5.4 KB. 98% reduction.

- Session Continuity — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. # Spec Guardian

Let formal specs test AI implementations.

A FizzBee spec describes the state transitions your system allows. However, the spec does not test whether your implementation follows those transitions. SpecGuardian turns FizzBee's results into tests that check whether your implementation reaches an allowed state.

SpecGuardian lets you verify that an AI-generated implementation actually conforms to your specification.

## From Spec to Test: Cache-Aside

In this cache-aside example, a WriteAndInvalidate action stores a new value in the database, then invalidates the corresponding cache entry. The tutorial spec models each operation as atomic and allows a crash before or between them:

@ conformance role CacheAside : fair action WriteAndInvalidate : # Yield to allow a crash before the first I/O. atomic : pass # Write to the database first, then invalidate the cache. db . write ( self . key , self . write_value ) cache . delete_cache ( self . key )

SpecGuardian generates Go tests from FizzBee's results. They compare the observed state after the action with states allowed by the spec, including states reached when an I/O operation fails.

For example, the generated Go test injects an error into the implementation just before cache invalidation, then checks whether the resulting state is allowed by the spec.

### Catching a Spec Mismatch

Consider an ordering bug in WriteAndInvalidate : cache invalidation runs before the database write.

func (ca *CacheAside) WriteAndInvalidate(ctx context.Context, input *Input) (*Output, error) { + if err := ca.cache.Delete(ctx, input.Key); err != nil { + return nil, err + } + if err := ca.db.Write(ctx, input.Key, input.Value); err != nil { return nil, err } - if err := ca.cache.Delete(ctx, input.Key); err != nil { - return nil, err - } - return &Output{Key: input.Key, Value: input.Value}, nil }

Both orders produce the same final state on success. But when the database write fails after cache invalidation, the database still holds old value and the cache entry is gone. The spec writes to the database first, so stopping at any point cannot produce this combination.

The test fails with the following output (excerpt):

actual state does not match any allowed state: I/O events: 1. valkey.Do 2. sql.BeginTx [fault injected; call not executed]

The mismatch excerpts show the unchanged database value and missing cache entry:

Fields.DB.Records[0].Value (-want +got): string( - "new", + "old", )

Fields.Cache.CachedRecords (-want +got): map[string]string{ - "cached": "old", }

## Getting Started

To try this example locally, start with the included cache-aside write tutorial. You'll need Go and Docker Compose; the FizzBee exploration results and generated tests are included.

Clone the repository and run the example:

git clone https://github.com/mrasu/spec-guardian.git cd spec-guardian/examples/tutorial_cache_aside_write docker compose up -d go test -count=1 -tags=specguardian ./conformance/...

The test passes, checking normal completion and injected I/O failures. Apply the diff above to cache_aside.go and rerun the go test command to reproduce the failure. Restore the original order to make the test pass again.

## How It Works

Here's how SpecGuardian works:

- FizzBee explores the possible states described by the spec.

- SpecGuardian generates Go tests from the exploration results.

- Either AI or you write the setup and Action execution code, configure providers in specguardian.yml , and write any remaining state observation code.

- The tests run a function normally and with an error injected immediately before a supported I/O call, then compare the observed state with states allowed by the spec.

specguardian.yml configures state observation and comparison. See the configuration schema for available settings and the example configuration for an example.

## When to Use

SpecGuardian checks whether an Action ends in a state allowed by the FizzBee spec, including after an injected I/O failure. It complements other tests:

- Different from unit tests: It checks the resulting application state against the spec, beyond assertions about individual functions.

- Different from integration tests: The expected states come from a FizzBee spec defined independently of the implementation.

## Generate Tests for Your Project

To generate tests for your project, install FizzBee and run these commands from your Go module directory:

fizz --output-dir path/to/output_dir path/to/YourSpec.fizz go get -tool github.com/mrasu/spec-guardian go tool spec-guardian init --fizzbee-output-dir path/to/output_dir # Configure observation and comparison. $EDITOR specguardian.yml go generate ./conformance # Replace <role> with the generated role name and connect the tests to your application. $EDITOR " conformance/specguardian/<role>_conformance_impl_test.go " go mod tidy go test -tags=specguardian ./conformance/...

See the user guide for the complete setup.

## Examples

- Cache-aside write tutorial is the completed project from the user guide .

- Cache-aside demonstrates the cache-aside pattern.

- Idempotent request demonstrates idempotent requests.

- Iceberg is a real-world example that tests apache/iceberg-go .

## Current Scope

SpecGuardian currently generates Go tests for one FizzBee Action invocation at a time. See the guardian directory for the available I/O hooks.

SpecGuardian is under development. Its public APIs or generated Go code may change.
